0.note: See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully, God, as I plead with you in prayer] or [Listen {to} my prayer, God! Indeed, do not hide yourself from my plea!]

The expressions **Listen** and **do not hide** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than a commands. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request in these cases and in the next verse. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make the meaning clear. Alternate translation: [Please listen … and please do not hide]

David is speaking as if God might actually **hide** himself so that David could not find him and make a **plea** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not disregard my plea]

2.note: In this context, the expression **answer me** means more than “say something in response to me.” It means “do what I ask.” In this case, David is asking God specifically to protect him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and protect me]

David is using a verbal form in which he is addressing himself and suggesting a course of action. (It is common in psalms of supplication for the psalmist to move back and forth between calling to God for help and making observations to himself about his own situation.) If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this with the same kind of statement form that David uses in the first part of this sentence when he says **I am restless**. Alternate translation: [and I moan]

3.note: David is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means all of the enemies who are threatening him on this occasion, as his use of the plural pronoun **they** later in this verse indicates. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from the voice of my enemies]

Here a person’s **voice** represents what he is saying by using his voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because of what my enemies are saying]

David is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the oppression of the wicked]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [because of the oppression of wicked people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because wicked people are oppressing me]

Here the expression **For** introduces more detailed information about what David’s wicked enemies are doing. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly in your translation. Alternate translation: [You see,]

David is speaking as if **trouble** were an object such as a large rock that his enemies could **shake** loose so that it would fall **onto** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [they stir up trouble for me] or [they trouble me greatly]
Here the **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in anger]

The verb that the ULT translates here as **persecute** means generally to “hold a grudge.” The focus in this context is not on an inner feeling of resentment but on a relentless attempt by someone holding a grudge to harm another person. If your language has a verb or phrase that describes this action, it would be appropriate to use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [they try relentlessly to harm me] or [they pursue a vendetta against me]

4.note: This statement could have a figurative meaning or a literal meaning or both. If your language has a term such as “heart” that describes an internal organ and can also represent emotions, it would be appropriate to use it here in your translation. This could mean: (1) that David is using his **heart** to represent his emotions. Alternate translation: [I feel very distressed inside] or (2) that David is describing physical symptoms that he is experiencing. Alternate translation: [My heart is pounding inside me] or [My heart is racing fast]

David is speaking as if the **terrors of death** were actually objects that could have **fallen onto** him. He means that he is feeling them immediately and forcefully, as if they had struck him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I feel the terrors of death strikingly]

David may be using the plural form **terrors**: (1) to indicate that the prospect of dying is making him feel a combination of fears. Alternate translation: [I feel strikingly all the fears that the prospect of dying makes a person feel] or (2) to emphasize that the fear of death is a very great fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a singular form and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I feel strikingly the great fear of death]

5.note: David is speaking of **Fear and trembling** as if they were living things that could have **come** upon him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I cannot help feeling afraid and trembling]
David is speaking as if **horror** had physically **covered** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and horror has overwhelmed me]

6.note: David has not **said** this to anyone else. He has said it to himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have said to myself] or [I have thought]

Here the word **wing** is singular in form, but it refers to both of the two wings that a dove has. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural or dual form of “wing.” Alternate translation: [Who will give, the wings of a dove are to me?]

David is using **Who will give** as a common expression of his culture to introduce a fervent wish. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O that I had the wings of a dove!] or [I fervently wish that I had the wings of a dove!]

David means implicitly that he wishes he could **dwell** somewhere safe. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and let me dwell somewhere safe]

7.note: David is using the term **Behold** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

The verbs **make distance** and **wandering** together express a single idea. The verb **wandering** tells in what way David would **make distance** between himself and his enemies. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [I would wander far away]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 19, see how your translation team decided to represent that term in 3:2.

8.note: Here, **an escape** represents “a place of escape.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to a place of escape] or [to a place where I am safe]

The terms **storming wind** and **tempest** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from the raging tempest]

David is speaking as if the hostile opposition of his wicked enemies were actually a **storming wind** or **tempest**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from these looming calamities]

9.note: The verb that the ULT translates as **Swallow** means “to swallow” in every other instance in the Hebrew Bible. (For example, Jonah 1:17, “Yahweh appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah.”) However, many biblical scholars believe, based on languages similar to Hebrew, that there was another verb with the same consonants that meant “confuse” and that David was using that verb here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [Confuse, Lord, divide their tongue] or [Lord, confuse and divide their tongue]

If this verb means **Swallow**, then David is speaking as if he wants the **Lord** actually to eat his enemies and swallow them. See how you translated the similar term “devour” in 35:25. Alternate translation: [Destroy them]

Here the word **tongue** is singular in form, but it refers to the tongues of all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “tongue.” Alternate translation: [divide their tongues]

David is using the term **tongue** to represent what his enemies would by using their tongues. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [make them disagree in what they say]
Here the word **For** introduces an explanation for what David asks in the previous sentence. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear.

The terms **violence** and **strife** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [much violence]
To decide whether to be more specific in your translation about what **city** David is referring to, see the discussion in the introduction to this psalm of when and why he probably wrote it.

10.note: David is referring to all of time by naming its two major components, **Day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All the time] or [Constantly]

David is speaking of the “violence” and “strife” he mentioned in the previous verse (referring back to them here as **they**) as if they were living things that could **go around** on the walls of a city. He is speaking of them as if they were watchmen who were supposed to make sure that there was good order in the city but who instead are making sure that there is continual fighting in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is violence all around the city]

David is speaking of **iniquity** and **trouble** as if they were living things that could dwell **in the midst of** a city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and wicked people cause trouble in the midst of it]

11.note: David is speaking of **oppression** and **deceit** as if they were living things that could **depart** from the open square of a city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and oppression and deceit are continually present in it]

12.note: Here the expression **For** introduces more detailed information about the identify of one of David’s enemies. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly in your translation. Alternate translation: [You see,]

13.note: Here and in the next verse, David addresses this former **companion** directly, even though he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to himself and to anyone who hears this song that he feels very strongly about how this former friend has betrayed him. If it would be helpful in your language, here and in the next verse you could translate what David says to this former friend as if he were speaking to other people about him. Alternate translation: [But it was a man according to my valuation, my companion and my acquaintance]

David is speaking as if someone had vowed both him and his former friend to God (as Leviticus 27:1–8 describes) and a priest had determined that they had the same **valuation**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a man equal to me]

Since David was the king of Israel, this **man** could not have been his actual equal in rank. David is probably describing the regard in which he held this man. Alternate translation: [a man whom I esteemed as my equal]

To decide whether to be more specific in your translation about what **companion** and **acquaintance** David is referring to, see the discussion in the introduction to this psalm of when and why he probably wrote it.

14.note: By **we** in both instances, David means himself and his former friend, whom he is addressing, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction. However, if you translated verse 13 as if David were speaking about his friend rather than to him, then **we** would not include the people to whom he is speaking (anyone else hearing this song), so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

David is speaking as if he and his former friend had actually **made** the **counsel** they formerly shared together **sweet**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we who spoke together very pleasantly]

David is speaking as if God’s temple were actually a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Since only priests could enter the temple building, David is referring to the courtyard of the temple. Alternate translation: [in the courtyard of the temple of God]

15.q: ישימות עָלֵ֗י⁠מוֹ יֵרְד֣וּ שְׁא֣וֹל חַיִּ֑ים כִּֽי־רָע֖וֹת בִּ⁠מְגוּרָ֣⁠ם בְּ⁠קִרְבָּֽ⁠ם
15.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because evils {are} in their dwelling, in the midst of them, may desolations be upon them; may they go down to Sheol alive]

The pronouns **them** and **they** refer to the enemies whom David first described in verse 3. He is talking about them as a group again after focusing on a specific one of them in verses 12–14. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May desolations be upon my enemies; may they go down]

This phrase is a translation of the written Hebrew text. Later Hebrew scribes, however, have recommended a correction in the margin of the text. You may want to follow this correction in your translation. Alternate translation: [May death seize upon them]

If this is the correct reading, David would be speaking of **desolations** as if they were objects that could be **upon** his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May things happen to them that desolate them]

If the correct reading is “May death seize upon them,” David would be speaking of death as if it were a living thing that could seize his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May they die without being able to resist dying]

David is alluding to the episode described in Numbers 16:1–33 in which men named Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebelled against Moses, and Yahweh judged and punished them by having the ground open up so that they “went down to Sheol alive.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [may they go down to Sheol alive, just like the people who rebelled against Moses]

David is speaking as if **evils** actually lived with his enemies in their **dwelling**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [evil is at home with them] or [they live in an environment that is constantly evil]

Here the word **dwelling** is singular in form, but it refers to the dwellings of all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “dwelling.” Alternate translation: [are in their dwellings]

16.note: David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will call** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what his enemies are doing (living wickedly, without regard for God), and what he will do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I will call to God]

17.note: David is referring to an entire day by naming three significant times in it, **Evening** (probably meaning sundown), **morning** (probably meaning dawn), and **noon**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Throughout the day]

David is using the term **voice** to represent what he would say by using his voice. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will hear what I say]

David is using the term **hear** to mean that God will do what he is asking him to do, as he states confidently in the next verse. The meaning of “hear” is the same in verse 19. Alternate translation: [and he will do what I ask]

18.note: David is speaking as if God actually **redeems** him or pays a price to free him from slavery or captivity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He rescues my life in peace from the battle against me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. In this context, that term has the sense of “well-being.” Alternate translation: [He rescues me, alive and well, from the battle against me]
The pronoun **they** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [my enemies are]

19.note: This phrase is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since in contexts like this, the term “answer” usually means “do what they ask” (as in verse 2). You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [and afflict them]

David is referring specifically to God **sitting** on his throne, and he is using that action to represent God ruling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the one enthroned] or [the one ruling]

The relative pronoun **whom** refers to David’s enemies. It may be more natural in your language to use a personal pronoun and begin a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [There are no changes to them]

By **changes**, David means misfortunes, losses, and disappointments in life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [They have no reversals of fortune] or [They enjoy continuous prosperity]

20.note: The pronoun **He** refers to David’s former friend. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My former friend stretches out]

David is using **stretches out his hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean “commits violent acts.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My former friend lays violent hands on his friends] or [My former friend commits violent acts against his friends]

The word “defile” means to treat something sacred as if it were common. The implication is that this former friend did not consider his **covenant** with David a sacred obligation that God would enforce. (David could be referring to a formal covenant or the implicit obligations of friendship.) As a result, he was not concerned that God would punish him if he broke the covenant. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he breaks his covenant] or [he disregards the obligations of friendship]

21.note: David is speaking as if the things that this former friend said with his **mouth** had actually been **curds**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [The things that he said were so smooth, it was as if they were curds] or [What he said caused no concern, just as a person can swallow curds without difficulty because they are smooth]

David is speaking as if this former friend’s **heart**, which represents his feelings, had actually been **war**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but secretly he felt hostile toward me]

The point of this comparison is that while soft olive **oil** is soothing to the skin, the **words** of this former friend were even more soothing and reassuring to David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [His words were even more soothing to me than soft olive oil is to the skin]

David is speaking as if this former friend’s words had actually been **swords** that soldiers had **unsheathed** so that they were ready to use. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but they were actually dangerous and deadly]

The expression **unsheathed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [were bare swords]

22.note: The words **you** and **your** and the implied “you” in the imperative **Cast** are singular because David is addressing himself and any individual in a similar situation who hears this song. So, use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

David is speaking of the difficulties that a person might have as if they were actually a **burden** that a person was carrying and that he could **Cast** onto **Yahweh** so that he would carry it instead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Trust Yahweh to help you with your difficulties]

David is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will sustain** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role that Yahweh will take in sustaining a person who trusts him. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and he will personally sustain you]

David is using the image of **shaking** something loose so that it falls from its position (he uses the same image in verse 3) to represent other people ruining righteous people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [he will not let the righteous down] or [he will not allow anyone to ruin the righteous]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [he will not allow shaking to righteous people] or [he will not allow anyone to ruin righteous people]

23.note: David is using the term **grave** to represent the decay and destruction of physical bodies that occurs in a grave. By characterizing this **pit** in that way, he is indicating that it is the chasm beneath the earth where his culture understood dead people to be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the pit of destruction] or [to the pit where dead people go]

Here, **blood** represents violently shedding blood. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Men of bloodshed and treachery] or [Murderous, treacherous men]

David is using **will not halve their days** as a common expression of his culture to mean “will not even live half as long as they otherwise would have.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will not reach middle age] or [will not even live half as long as they otherwise would have]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will trust** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what will happen to the wicked people he has just described and what he will do himself. Alternate translation: [But for my part, I will trust]
